Lab 4 Demo: Monte Carlo Simulation¶

SCIM211 Simulation Modelling — self-study notes

These notes cover the theory and Python you need for Lab 4. Read each section, run the code cells in order, and look carefully at every intermediate value. When you meet a Question or Predict, stop and write down your own answer before reading on or running the next cell.

Topics:

  1. the Monte Carlo estimator of $I=\mathbb E[h(X)]$;
  2. the Law of Large Numbers (LLN);
  3. variance, sample standard deviation;
  4. standard deviation versus standard error;
  5. the Central Limit Theorem (CLT);
  6. the approximate 95% confidence interval and what "95%" means;
  7. the $O(n^{-1/2})$ convergence rate, and the difference between Monte Carlo error and model error;
  8. estimating a probability by averaging an indicator.

Part 0: Setup¶

In [1]:
import numpy as npimport pandas as pdimport matplotlib.pyplot as pltimport mathDEMO_SEED = 6901

Random number generators and seeds¶

A computer does not produce "truly" random numbers. It produces a pseudo-random stream: a long deterministic sequence that behaves statistically like independent Uniform(0,1) numbers.

  • np.random.default_rng(seed) creates a generator object — think of it as a machine that holds our position in one particular stream.
  • The seed chooses which stream. Same seed → same stream → same numbers → reproducible results.
  • Each time we ask the generator for numbers, it moves forward in the stream. It does not go back unless we create a new generator with the same seed.
In [2]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)rng.random(3)
Out[2]:
array([0.01616044, 0.14851885, 0.45906659])
In [3]:
rng.random(3)
Out[3]:
array([0.24609152, 0.07405111, 0.63003903])
In [4]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)rng.random(3)
Out[4]:
array([0.01616044, 0.14851885, 0.45906659])

Question: Compare the outputs of the three cells above. Why does the second cell give different numbers from the first? Why does the third cell reproduce the first exactly?

Theory 1: What is Monte Carlo estimation?¶

Why we need it¶

Many quantities we care about are averages over randomness: expected profit of a shop, expected waiting time in a queue, the probability that a system fails. Often we can simulate the random system easily, but we cannot calculate the average exactly. Monte Carlo says: simulate many times and average.

The formal set-up¶

Every Monte Carlo problem in this lab has the same three ingredients.

SymbolNameMeaning
$X$random inputEverything random that goes into one run of the model (one number, or a whole vector of numbers).
$h(X)$model outputThe number the model produces from that input. Since $X$ is random, $h(X)$ is a random variable.
$I=\mathbb E[h(X)]$targetThe true long-run average output. It is a fixed number, usually unknown.

We write $Y=h(X)$ for the output. The target is

$$I=\mathbb E[Y]=\mathbb E[h(X)].$$

The estimator¶

Generate iid inputs $X_1,\dots,X_n$, each with the same distribution as $X$. Compute the outputs

$$Y_i=h(X_i),\qquad i=1,\dots,n,$$

and average them:

$$\boxed{\;\hat I_n=\bar Y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\;}$$

Target versus estimate¶

$I$$\hat I_n$
What is it?the population / true meanthe simulated sample mean
Random?No — a fixed numberYes — changes if we use different random numbers
Known?usually notyes, we compute it

Why should averaging random outputs recover $I$?¶

Intuition: each $Y_i$ is "$I$ plus noise". Some noises are positive, some negative. When we average many of them, the positive and negative noises largely cancel, and what is left is close to $I$. The Law of Large Numbers (Theory 2) makes this precise; the Central Limit Theorem (Theory 5) tells us how close.

Two examples with the same structure¶

Integration exampleKiosk example
Input $X$$U\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$today's random demand and each customer's random spend
Output $h(X)$$e^U$today's profit
Target$\mathbb E[e^U]=\int_0^1e^u\,du$expected daily profit $\mathbb E[H]$
Estimatoraverage of $e^{U_i}$average of simulated daily profits

The mathematics is identical. Only the model $h$ changes.

Questions: For each item, is it a random input, a fixed parameter, a model output, or a target?

  1. The number of customers who arrive tomorrow.
  2. The fixed rent of the kiosk.
  3. Tomorrow's profit.
  4. The long-run average daily profit.
  5. The average profit over 1,000 simulated days.

Demo 1: Monte Carlo integration — one small sample, by hand¶

The mathematical idea¶

We want

$$I=\int_0^1 e^x\,dx = e-1\approx 1.71828.$$

We know the answer exactly, which is why this is a good test problem: we can check Monte Carlo against the truth.

Why is this integral an expectation? If $U\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$, its density is $f_U(u)=1$ for $0<u<1$. For any function $h$,

$$\mathbb E[h(U)]=\int_0^1 h(u)\,f_U(u)\,du=\int_0^1 h(u)\cdot 1\,du .$$

With $h(u)=e^u$:

$$I=\int_0^1 e^u\,du=\mathbb E[e^U].$$

So: $X=U$, $h(X)=e^U$, and the Monte Carlo estimator is

$$\hat I_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n e^{U_i}.$$

Predict: If we average only 10 values of $e^{U_i}$, will we get exactly $1.71828$? Roughly how far off might we be?

Step 1 — generate a small sample of uniforms and look at them¶

Step 4 — the average, piece by piece¶

The sample mean is

$$\bar h=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n h_i}{n}.$$

We compute the numerator, the denominator, and then the ratio, in separate cells.

estimate = h_small.mean()exact_integral = np.e - 1print("Monte Carlo estimate :", estimate)print("Exact integral e - 1 :", exact_integral)
Monte Carlo estimate : 1.4734937845313343Exact integral e - 1 : 1.718281828459045

Step 5 — how wrong are we? Signed error versus absolute error¶

$$\text{error}=\hat I_n - I, \qquad \text{absolute error}=|\hat I_n-I|.$$

  • The signed error tells us the direction: negative means we underestimated, positive means we overestimated.
  • The absolute error tells us only the size of the mistake. It is what we plot when we ask "how close are we?".
In [13]:
error = estimate - exact_integralerror
Out[13]:

In [14]:
absolute_error = abs(error)absolute_error

Questions:

  1. If we rerun only the cell u_small = rng.random(10) without re-creating rng, should the estimate change?
  2. Would it be surprising if another sample of 10 gave an error of $+0.2$?

Note. The whole of Monte Carlo is in these few cells: random inputs → model outputs → average. Everything that follows is about (a) why the average works and (b) how much to trust it.

Theory 2: The Law of Large Numbers (LLN)¶

Intuition¶

One output $Y_i$ can be far from $I$. The average of many outputs is much more stable, because positive and negative deviations cancel. The more outputs we average, the less room there is for a few unlucky values to drag the average away.

Theorem Statement¶

Let $Y_1,Y_2,\dots$ be iid with finite mean $\mu=\mathbb E[Y]$. Then

$$\bar Y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i \;\longrightarrow\; \mu \qquad\text{as } n\to\infty$$

(with probability 1 — this is the strong law; the weak law says $\mathbb P(|\bar Y_n-\mu|>\varepsilon)\to0$ for every $\varepsilon>0$).

Assumptions actually used: the $Y_i$ are independent, have the same distribution, and $\mathbb E|Y|<\infty$. In Monte Carlo we arrange the first two by design (independent random inputs, same model every time).

What the LLN does not say¶

  1. It does not say an individual $Y_i$ gets closer to $\mu$. Individual outputs stay exactly as random as before.
  2. It does not say the error $|\bar Y_n-\mu|$ decreases every time $n$ increases. Adding one more observation can move the average away from $\mu$.
  3. It does not tell us how large $n$ must be for a given accuracy. That is the job of the CLT.

The LLN is a statement about the long run.

In [15]:
lln_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED + 1)n_max = 10000y_lln = np.exp(lln_rng.random(n_max))n_values = np.arange(1, n_max + 1)running_mean = np.cumsum(y_lln) / n_valuesrunning_abs_error = np.abs(running_mean - exact_integral)running_mean[:5]
Out[15]:
array([2.12774476, 1.68011275, 1.50180046, 1.51759442, 1.4992915 ])
In [16]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))axes[0].plot(n_values, y_lln, ".", markersize=1, alpha=0.3, color="grey", label="individual outputs $Y_i$")axes[0].plot(n_values, running_mean, color="C0", label=r"running average $\bar Y_n$")axes[0].axhline(exact_integral, color="black", linestyle="--", label="$e-1$")axes[0].set_xscale("log")axes[0].set_xlabel("n")axes[0].set_title("Outputs stay random; the average settles")axes[0].legend()axes[1].plot(n_values, running_abs_error, color="C1")axes[1].set_xscale("log")axes[1].set_yscale("log")axes[1].set_xlabel("n")axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$|\bar Y_n-(e-1)|$")axes[1].set_title("Absolute error: shrinks overall, but NOT monotonically")plt.tight_layout()plt.show()

One more look: three independent runs of the same experiment. Each path is a different random stream.

In [18]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))path_rng = np.random.default_rng(1)path_mean = np.cumsum(np.exp(path_rng.random(n_max))) / n_valuesax.plot(n_values, path_mean, label="seed 1")path_rng = np.random.default_rng(2)path_mean = np.cumsum(np.exp(path_rng.random(n_max))) / n_valuesax.plot(n_values, path_mean, label="seed 2")path_rng = np.random.default_rng(3)path_mean = np.cumsum(np.exp(path_rng.random(n_max))) / n_valuesax.plot(n_values, path_mean, label="seed 3")ax.axhline(exact_integral, color="black", linestyle="--", label="$e-1$")ax.set_xscale("log")ax.set_xlabel("n")ax.set_ylabel(r"$\bar Y_n$")ax.set_title("Different random streams, same limit")ax.legend()plt.show()

Different streams give different paths — the estimate is random — but all paths approach the same fixed target.

The LLN tells us where the average goes. It does not yet tell us how far from the target a path typically is at, say, $n=100$. For that we need variance.

Theory 3: Variance and sample standard deviation¶

Population quantities (fixed, usually unknown)¶

$$\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E\big[(Y-\mu)^2\big],\qquad \sigma=\sqrt{\sigma^2}.$$

$\sigma$ measures how spread out individual outputs are around their mean.

Sample quantities (computed from simulated data)¶

$$s^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\big(Y_i-\bar Y\big)^2,\qquad s=\sqrt{s^2}.$$

Why $n-1$ and not $n$?¶

We do not know $\mu$, so we measure deviations from $\bar Y$ instead. But $\bar Y$ is computed from the same data, and it is the number that makes $\sum(Y_i-c)^2$ as small as possible over all choices of $c$. So deviations from $\bar Y$ are, on average, a little too small compared with deviations from the true $\mu$. Dividing by $n-1$ instead of $n$ corrects this exactly: one can show $\mathbb E[s^2]=\sigma^2$ (for iid data with finite variance). Informally, after using the data once to estimate $\bar Y$, only $n-1$ of the deviations are "free" — they must add up to zero — hence "degrees of freedom".

What ddof means in NumPy¶

values.std(ddof=d) computes

$$\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-d}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)^2 }.$$

  • ddof=0 (NumPy's default) divides by $n$: the SD of the numbers treated as a whole population.
  • ddof=1 divides by $n-1$: the sample SD, $s$. This is what we want, because our simulated outputs are a sample from the model.

Warning: pandas uses ddof=1 by default (Series.std()), while NumPy uses ddof=0 by default (array.std()). Always write ddof=1 explicitly with NumPy.

Theory 4: Standard deviation versus standard error¶

This is the most important distinction in the lab. We will return to it repeatedly.

Standard deviation $s$ (or $\sigma$)Standard error $\mathrm{SE}(\bar Y)$
Measures variation of …individual outputs $Y_i$the estimated mean $\bar Y_n$
Question it answers"How different is one simulated day from another?""If I redid the whole simulation, how much would my answer move?"
As $n$ increasessettles to $\sigma$ — does not shrink to 0shrinks like $1/\sqrt n$

Variance of a sample mean¶

Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be independent, each with variance $\sigma^2$. Two facts:

  • $\mathrm{Var}(cZ)=c^2\,\mathrm{Var}(Z)$ for a constant $c$;
  • for independent (in fact, uncorrelated suffices) random variables, $\mathrm{Var}(Z_1+\dots+Z_n)=\mathrm{Var}(Z_1)+\dots+\mathrm{Var}(Z_n)$.

Therefore

$$\mathrm{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\right)=\frac1{n^2}\,\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i\right)=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)=\frac1{n^2}\cdot n\sigma^2=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},$$

and so

$$\boxed{\;\mathrm{SD}(\bar Y_n)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\;}$$

The step $\mathrm{Var}(\sum Y_i)=\sum\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)$ is exactly where independence is used. If replications were not independent (for example, if we accidentally reused the same random numbers), this formula would be wrong.

Estimated standard error¶

$\sigma$ is unknown, so we plug in the sample SD:

$$\mathrm{SE}=\frac{s}{\sqrt n}.$$

Intuition¶

Averaging $n$ independent noisy values cancels noise, but not perfectly: the noise in the sum grows like $\sqrt n$ (not like $n$), while we divide by $n$. Net effect: $\sqrt n/n=1/\sqrt n$.

Question: As $n$ increases, which quantity should shrink towards 0: the SD of the outputs, or the SE of the mean?

Theory 5: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)¶

Why we need it¶

The LLN says $\bar Y_n\to\mu$. But in practice we stop at some finite $n$ and must report how far off we might be. For that we need to know the distribution of the error $\bar Y_n-\mu$. The CLT supplies it.

A new idea: the sampling distribution¶

$\bar Y_n$ is computed from random outputs, so $\bar Y_n$ is itself a random variable. Imagine repeating the entire Monte Carlo experiment (all $n$ replications) many times, each time with fresh random numbers, and recording the $\bar Y_n$ from each experiment. The distribution of those recorded means is called the sampling distribution of the estimator.

  • One observation from the distribution of $Y$ = one replication (one $e^{U}$, one simulated day).
  • One observation from the sampling distribution of $\bar Y_n$ = one whole experiment of $n$ replications.

Statement¶

Let $Y_1,Y_2,\dots$ be iid with mean $\mu$ and finite variance $0<\sigma^2<\infty$. Then

$$Z_n=\frac{\bar Y_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\;\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\;N(0,1),$$

which means $\mathbb P(Z_n\le z)\to\Phi(z)$ for every $z$, where $\Phi$ is the standard Normal CDF. Informally, for sufficiently large $n$,

$$\bar Y_n\;\approx\;N\!\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).$$

The same limit holds if we replace the unknown $\sigma$ by the sample SD $s$ (because $s\to\sigma$ by the LLN; the formal tool is Slutsky's theorem). This is what licenses using $s/\sqrt n$ in practice.

Remarks¶

  1. The original output $Y$ does not need to be Normal. $e^U$ is not Normal (it is not even symmetric), and daily profit need not be Normal. The CLT is about the average, not the individual values.
  2. It is the sampling distribution of $\bar Y_n$ that becomes approximately Normal — the histogram of many repeated means, not the histogram of outputs.
  3. "Sufficiently large $n$" is not a fixed number. The more skewed or heavy-tailed $Y$ is, the larger $n$ must be. For the smooth, bounded $e^U$, $n=100$ is plenty; for a rare-event indicator it may not be.
  4. The CLT needs finite variance. (Every model in this lab satisfies this.)

LLN versus CLT¶

LLNCLT
Tells uswhere $\bar Y_n$ goeshow $\bar Y_n$ is spread around where it goes
Formula$\bar Y_n\to\mu$$\dfrac{\bar Y_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\approx N(0,1)$
Licenses the statement"the answer is right in the long run""here is an error bar for this $n$"

We will see the CLT in Demo 3 by repeating an experiment 500 times.

Theory 6: The approximate 95% confidence interval¶

Where 1.96 comes from¶

For $Z\sim N(0,1)$,

$$\mathbb P(-1.96<Z<1.96)\approx0.95 ,$$

equivalently $\Phi(1.96)\approx0.975$: 2.5% in each tail. Let us check this two ways — with an exact formula, and with Monte Carlo itself.

In [19]:
math.erf(1.96 / np.sqrt(2))
Out[19]:
0.9500042097035591
In [20]:
z_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED + 3)z_draws = z_rng.standard_normal(1_000_000)inside = (z_draws > -1.96) & (z_draws < 1.96)inside.mean()
Out[20]:
np.float64(0.949619)

From the CLT to the interval¶

By the CLT, approximately,

$$\mathbb P\!\left(-1.96<\frac{\bar Y_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}<1.96\right)\approx0.95 .$$

Multiply through by $\sigma/\sqrt n$ and rearrange the inequalities so that $\mu$ is in the middle:

$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bar Y_n-1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}<\mu<\bar Y_n+1.96\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right)\approx0.95 .$$

Replace $\sigma$ by $s$:

$$\boxed{\;\bar Y_n\pm1.96\,\frac{s}{\sqrt n}\;}$$

The parts of the interval¶

NameFormulaMeaning
estimate$\bar Y_n$our best single guess of $\mu$
standard error$\mathrm{SE}=s/\sqrt n$typical size of the estimation error
margin of error$1.96\times\mathrm{SE}$half-width of the interval
lower endpoint$\bar Y_n-1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$
upper endpoint$\bar Y_n+1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$
width$2\times1.96\,\mathrm{SE}$total length of the interval

What "95%" means¶

Look carefully at the probability statement above: the random quantities are $\bar Y_n$ and $s$, i.e. the endpoints. The target $\mu$ is fixed.

If we repeated the entire procedure many times — new random numbers, new $\bar Y_n$, new $s$, new interval — then about 95% of the intervals constructed this way would contain the true mean $\mu$.

Once we have computed one interval, say $[1.19, 1.76]$, it either contains $\mu$ or it does not. The 95% is a property of the procedure, not of one particular interval. We will check this by simulation in Demo 3.

A CI for the mean is not a range for individual outputs¶

The CI is about $\mu=\mathbb E[Y]$. It is not a range that contains 95% of individual outputs $Y_i$. Individual outputs are spread with SD $\sigma$; the CI has half-width $1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n$, which is far smaller when $n$ is large. Confusing these two is the most common error in Lab 4 recommendations.

Now repeat the whole calculation for a larger sample¶

We now want the same numbers for $n=10$ and $n=100$. First we do it the long way: copy the calculation and change $n$.

n = 10: estimate = 1.4735, SD = 0.4613, SE = 0.1459, CI = [1.1876, 1.7594]
In [31]:
n = 100u = rng.random(n)h_values = np.exp(u)estimate = h_values.mean()sample_sd = h_values.std(ddof=1)standard_error = sample_sd / np.sqrt(n)margin = 1.96 * standard_errorprint(f"n = {n}: estimate = {estimate:.4f}, SD = {sample_sd:.4f}, SE = {standard_error:.4f}, "      f"CI = [{estimate - margin:.4f}, {estimate + margin:.4f}]")
n = 100: estimate = 1.7094, SD = 0.5239, SE = 0.0524, CI = [1.6068, 1.8121]

We are about to repeat exactly the same calculation for $n=1000$ and $n=10000$. Copying the block again and again is tedious, and dangerous: if we fix a mistake in one copy we must remember to fix it in every copy. This repeated structure is why a loop is useful.

Note that the second block did not re-create rng, so the 100 uniforms for $n=100$ are the next 100 numbers in the stream, not the first 10 again.

Python: the for loop¶

Start with a loop that does nothing but announce the value of n.

In [32]:
for n in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:    print("This time round the loop, n =", n)
This time round the loop, n = 10This time round the loop, n = 100This time round the loop, n = 1000This time round the loop, n = 10000

How to read it:

  • [10, 100, 1000, 10000] is a list: four values in order.
  • for n in ...: means "take the first value, call it n, run the indented block; then take the next value, call it n, run the block again; … until the list is used up".
  • n is an ordinary variable. It is overwritten on each pass (iteration): 10, then 100, then 1000, then 10000.
  • The colon : ends the for line and says "the block follows".
  • The indentation (4 spaces) defines the block. Every indented line is repeated; the first line that is not indented is outside the loop and runs once, after the loop has finished.

Now the loop¶

Compare it line by line with the two manual blocks above: the body of the loop is the manual block, and the list replaces "change $n$ by hand".

In [33]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)integration_rows = []for n in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:    u = rng.random(n)    h_values = np.exp(u)    estimate = h_values.mean()    sample_sd = h_values.std(ddof=1)    standard_error = sample_sd / np.sqrt(n)    margin = 1.96 * standard_error    integration_rows.append({        "n": n,        "estimate": estimate,        "absolute_error": abs(estimate - exact_integral),        "sample_sd": sample_sd,        "standard_error": standard_error,        "lower": estimate - margin,        "upper": estimate + margin,        "ci_width": 2 * margin,    })

In [36]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))axes[0].errorbar(integration_demo["n"], integration_demo["estimate"],                 yerr=1.96 * integration_demo["standard_error"],                 marker="o", capsize=4, label="estimate ± 1.96 SE")axes[0].axhline(exact_integral, color="black", linestyle="--", label="exact value $e-1$")axes[0].set_xscale("log")axes[0].set_xlabel("Sample size n")axes[0].set_ylabel("Integral estimate")axes[0].set_title("LLN: estimates settle; intervals shrink")axes[0].legend()axes[1].plot(integration_demo["n"], integration_demo["ci_width"], marker="o", label="95% CI width")axes[1].plot(integration_demo["n"], integration_demo["sample_sd"], marker="s", label="sample SD s")axes[1].set_xscale("log")axes[1].set_yscale("log")axes[1].set_xlabel("Sample size n")axes[1].set_title("SD stays put; CI width shrinks like 1/sqrt(n)")axes[1].legend()plt.tight_layout()plt.show()

Interpretation.

  • On a log–log plot, a quantity proportional to $n^{-1/2}$ is a straight line of slope $-1/2$: every factor 10 in $n$ drops the width by a factor $\sqrt{10}\approx3.16$. The CI width follows that line; the SD is flat.
  • Reducing the SE by a factor of 10 needs about 100 times as many replications. Monte Carlo is reliable but slow.
  • A larger sample reduces the typical error. It does not guarantee that any particular larger-$n$ estimate is closer to the truth.

Demo 3: One estimate has a sampling distribution (seeing the CLT)¶

Question: "If I rerun the whole $n=100$ experiment with fresh uniforms, do I get the same answer? How different could it be?"

We answer this by actually doing it — first twice by hand, then a few times with a simple loop, and only then hundreds of times with a function.

Experiment A — 100 uniforms, one estimate¶

In [37]:
experiment_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED + 4)u_A = experiment_rng.random(100)estimate_A = np.exp(u_A).mean()print(f"Experiment A: estimate = {estimate_A:.5f}")
Experiment A: estimate = 1.66226

Experiment B — a fresh 100 uniforms, same method¶

In [38]:
u_B = experiment_rng.random(100)estimate_B = np.exp(u_B).mean()print(f"Experiment B: estimate = {estimate_B:.5f}")print(f"Difference A - B      = {estimate_A - estimate_B:.5f}")
Experiment B: estimate = 1.68096Difference A - B      = -0.01871

Question: Why are the two estimates different if they are estimating the same quantity?

The real function: one row per repeated experiment¶

repeated_estimates repeats the whole $n$-sample experiment many times and records, for each repetition, the estimate, its standard error and its confidence interval.

In [39]:
def repeated_estimates(n, repeats, rng, z=1.96):    """Repeat the whole n-sample Monte Carlo experiment `repeats` times.    Returns a DataFrame with one row per experiment: estimate, SE and interval.    """    rows = []    for _ in range(repeats):        u = rng.random(n)        h = np.exp(u)        estimate = h.mean()        standard_error = h.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)        rows.append({            "estimate": estimate,            "standard_error": standard_error,            "lower": estimate - z * standard_error,            "upper": estimate + z * standard_error,        })    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
  • Parameters: n (replications per experiment), repeats (how many experiments), rng (the generator to draw from), z (critical value, default 1.96).
  • for _ in range(repeats): — we need to repeat repeats times but never use the counter, so by convention we name it _.
  • Why is rng an argument, not created inside? If the function did rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED) inside the loop, every experiment would use the same 100 uniforms and all rows would be identical. Passing one generator in lets it move forward through the stream, so each experiment gets new random numbers, while the whole run is still reproducible from the one seed chosen outside.

Always test a new function on a tiny case first. Three experiments of size 10:

In [40]:
tiny_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED + 5)repeated_estimates(n=10, repeats=3, rng=tiny_rng)

Question: What does one row represent? Why do the three intervals differ in both centre and width?

What does the CLT predict for this problem? — derive $\sigma$ exactly¶

For $Y=e^U$, $U\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$:

Mean.$$\mathbb E[Y]=\int_0^1e^u\,du=e-1\approx1.718282.$$

Second moment.$$\mathbb E[Y^2]=\mathbb E[e^{2U}]=\int_0^1e^{2u}\,du=\left[\tfrac12e^{2u}\right]_0^1=\frac{e^2-1}{2}\approx3.194528.$$

Variance.$$\sigma^2=\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mathbb E[Y^2]-(\mathbb E[Y])^2=\frac{e^2-1}{2}-(e-1)^2\approx0.242036,\qquad \sigma\approx0.491971 .$$

Prediction for the sampling distribution.$$\mathrm{SD}(\bar Y_{100})=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{100}}=\frac{\sigma}{10}\approx0.049197,\qquad\mathrm{SD}(\bar Y_{400})=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{400}}=\frac{\sigma}{20}\approx0.024599 .$$

Going from $n=100$ to $n=400$ multiplies $n$ by 4, so the SD should be multiplied by $1/\sqrt4=\tfrac12$:

$$n\times4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathrm{SE}\times\tfrac12 .$$

This is a falsifiable prediction. Let us test it.

In [41]:
E_Y = np.e - 1E_Y2 = (np.e ** 2 - 1) / 2var_h = E_Y2 - E_Y ** 2sigma_h = np.sqrt(var_h)pd.Series({    "E[Y] = e - 1": E_Y,    "E[Y^2] = (e^2 - 1)/2": E_Y2,    "Var(Y)": var_h,    "sigma = SD(Y)": sigma_h,    "predicted SD of estimate, n = 100": sigma_h / np.sqrt(100),    "predicted SD of estimate, n = 400": sigma_h / np.sqrt(400),})

The key picture: distribution of individual outputs vs distribution of repeated means¶

Question (think before running the next cell): In the left panel each observation is one $e^{U_i}$. In the right panel each observation is one whole experiment's average of 100 of them. Which will look more like a bell curve? Which will be wider?

In [46]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))axes[0].hist(y_lln, bins=40, density=True, color="grey", edgecolor="white",             label="10,000 individual outputs")y_grid = np.linspace(1, np.e, 200)axes[0].plot(y_grid, 1 / y_grid, color="black", label="exact density $1/y$ on $[1,e]$")axes[0].set_xlim(0.9, 2.8)axes[0].set_title(r"Individual outputs $Y=e^U$ (NOT Normal)")axes[0].set_xlabel("y")axes[0].set_ylabel("Density")axes[0].legend()axes[1].hist(repeated_estimates_100, bins=25, density=True, color="tab:blue", edgecolor="white",             label=r"500 estimates $\bar Y_{100}$")m_grid = np.linspace(1.55, 1.9, 300)predicted_sd = sigma_h / np.sqrt(100)normal_curve = np.exp(-0.5 * ((m_grid - exact_integral) / predicted_sd) ** 2) / (predicted_sd * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))axes[1].plot(m_grid, normal_curve, color="black", label=r"CLT: $N(e-1,\ \sigma^2/100)$")axes[1].axvline(exact_integral, color="black", linestyle="--")axes[1].set_title(r"Sampling distribution of $\bar Y_{100}$ (approx. Normal)")axes[1].set_xlabel("estimate")axes[1].legend()plt.tight_layout()plt.show()

Remarks.

  1. The left histogram is of outputs: $Y=e^U$ has density $1/y$ on $[1,e]$ (derive it yourself: $\mathbb P(Y\le y)=\mathbb P(U\le\ln y)=\ln y$, then differentiate). It is decreasing and skewed — nothing like a bell curve.
  2. The right histogram is of averages of 100 outputs. It is symmetric and bell-shaped, and the black curve is not fitted to the data — it is the CLT's prediction $N(e-1,\sigma^2/100)$ from the formula we derived. That is the Central Limit Theorem.
  3. Horizontal scales: the left spans about 1.7 units; the right spans about 0.3 units. The ratio of spreads is $\sqrt{100}=10$.

Question: Why can individual outputs be non-Normal while sample means look Normal?

Remarks.

  1. The intervals move; the target does not. Each horizontal line is one experiment's interval. The vertical dashed line never moves.
  2. About 95% of the 500 intervals contain the truth. Coverage is itself estimated from 500 intervals, so it has sampling error of about $\sqrt{0.95\times0.05/500}\approx0.01$. Values between roughly 0.93 and 0.97 are consistent with 95%; do not present 0.934 as a failure of the method.
  3. This is exactly what "95% confidence" means: a statement about the long-run behaviour of the procedure.

Question: "Which of these 500 answers would you have reported if you had run the experiment once?"

Lab link: Lab 4 Parts A2–A3 ask you to reproduce this for $\int_0^1x^2\,dx=1/3$, where $\sigma_h=\sqrt{4/45}\approx0.29814$.

Theory 7: The Monte Carlo convergence rate $O(n^{-1/2})$¶

The rate¶

$$\mathrm{SE}(\bar Y_n)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}=O\!\left(n^{-1/2}\right).$$

"$O(n^{-1/2})$" means: bounded by a constant times $n^{-1/2}$. Here the constant is $\sigma$ — it depends on the problem (how variable the output is), while the exponent $-1/2$ is the same for every Monte Carlo problem.

Practical consequences¶

Multiply the number of replications bySE is multiplied by
4$1/\sqrt4=1/2$
10$1/\sqrt{10}\approx0.316$
100$1/10$
10,000$1/100$

Each extra correct decimal place costs 100 times as many replications.

How many replications for a target precision?¶

To get a 95% half-width at most $\varepsilon$: $1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt n\le\varepsilon$, i.e.

$$n\;\ge\;\left(\frac{1.96\,\sigma}{\varepsilon}\right)^2 .$$

In [50]:
for target_half_width in [0.01, 0.001]:    n_needed = (1.96 * sigma_h / target_half_width) ** 2    print(f"half-width {target_half_width}: need n >= {n_needed:,.0f}")
half-width 0.01: need n >= 9,298half-width 0.001: need n >= 929,804

Two correct decimals cost about 9,300 replications; three cost about 930,000 — 100 times more.

More replications reduce Monte Carlo error. They do not repair a bad model.¶

There are two different kinds of uncertainty in any simulation study:

Monte Carlo (sampling) errorModel error
Sourcefinite number of random replicationswrong or simplified assumptions (distributions, parameters, missing features)
Measured bySE and CInot measured by SE or CI at all
Reduced bymore replicationsbetter data, validation, sensitivity analysis

A confidence interval says: "if the model is right, this is how precisely we have computed its expected output." It says nothing about whether the model is right.

Question: "If the model assumptions are wrong, will 1,000,000 replications fix them?"

Demo 4: From mathematical integration to a business decision¶

Monte Carlo does not change when the model becomes more realistic. Only $X$ and $h$ change.

$$X\;\longrightarrow\;h(X)$$

IntegrationKiosk
Random input $X$$U\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$today's demand $D$ and each customer's spend $S_1,\dots,S_D$
Model $h$$h(U)=e^U$$h(X)=\text{revenue}-\text{cost}=$ today's profit $H$
One replicationone uniformone simulated day
Target(s)$\mathbb E[e^U]$$\mathbb E[H]$ and $\mathbb P(H<0)$
Estimator$\frac1n\sum e^{U_i}$$\frac1n\sum H_i$ and $\frac1n\sum\mathbf 1\{H_i<0\}$

The decision¶

A campus smoothie kiosk is considering a digital coupon. It may attract more customers but lowers spend per customer and costs money to run. The decision uses two targets:

$$\mathbb E[H]\qquad\text{and}\qquad \mathbb P(H<0)=\mathbb E\big[\mathbf 1\{H<0\}\big].$$

The first measures expected return; the second measures downside frequency (how often the kiosk loses money). The second target is also an expectation — of an indicator — so the same Monte Carlo machinery applies (Demo 7).

ComponentRegular dayCoupon day
Demand $D$rounded Normal(70, 10), clipped at 0rounded Normal(86, 16), clipped at 0
Spend per customer $S_j$Normal(6.0, 0.8), clipped at 0Normal(5.7, 0.9), clipped at 0
Variable cost per customer2.52.5
Fixed cost180180
Campaign cost030

Question: Which entries are random inputs, which are fixed parameters, and which quantities are outputs?

Python lesson: dictionaries¶

We store each scenario's assumptions in a dictionary: a collection of key: value pairs, written inside { }. We look up a value by its key with square brackets, e.g. regular["demand_mean"].

In [51]:
regular = {    "demand_mean": 70,    "demand_sd": 10,    "spend_mean": 6.0,    "spend_sd": 0.8,    "variable_cost": 2.5,    "fixed_cost": 180,    "campaign_cost": 0,}coupon = {    "demand_mean": 86,    "demand_sd": 16,    "spend_mean": 5.7,    "spend_sd": 0.9,    "variable_cost": 2.5,    "fixed_cost": 180,    "campaign_cost": 30,}
In [52]:
regular["demand_mean"]
Out[52]:
70

Demo 5: Build one regular day by hand¶

This is the structural heart of the lab. In Lab 4 the daily-profit model is provided; you are not asked to build it, but you must be able to explain every line. So we build one day step by step, and only then package it into a function.

The model for one day:

$$D=\max\big(0,\ \mathrm{round}(N(\mu_D,\sigma_D))\big),\qquadS_j=\max\big(0,\ N(\mu_S,\sigma_S)\big),\ j=1,\dots,D,$$

$$R=\sum_{j=1}^{D}S_j,\qquadC=c_v D+C_{\text{fixed}}+C_{\text{campaign}},\qquadH=R-C.$$

In [53]:
manual_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)demand_mean = regular["demand_mean"]demand_sd = regular["demand_sd"]print("demand mean =", demand_mean, "   demand SD =", demand_sd)
demand mean = 70    demand SD = 10

Demand, one operation at a time¶

Step 1 — raw Normal draw. A Normal random variable is continuous: it gives numbers like 73.02, not whole customers.

In [54]:
raw_demand = manual_rng.normal(demand_mean, demand_sd)raw_demand
Out[54]:
73.02264359400246

Step 2 — round to the nearest whole number. Customers come in whole numbers.

In [55]:
rounded_demand = round(raw_demand)rounded_demand
Out[55]:
73

Step 3 — make sure the result is an integer type. In current Python, round(x) already returns an integer, but some older NumPy versions returned a float such as 73.0. The next step uses demand as an array size, which must be an integer, so the model code writes int(...) explicitly as a safeguard.

In [56]:
integer_demand = int(rounded_demand)print(integer_demand, type(raw_demand), type(integer_demand))
73 <class 'float'> <class 'int'>

Step 4 — clip at zero. A Normal draw can in principle be negative, but negative customers make no sense (and NumPy refuses a negative array size). max(0, d) returns the larger of 0 and $d$: it leaves positive values alone and replaces negatives by 0.

In [57]:
demand = max(0, integer_demand)demand
Out[57]:
73
In [58]:
print("max(0, 73) =", max(0, 73), "   max(0, -4) =", max(0, -4))print("round(2.5) =", round(2.5), "   round(3.5) =", round(3.5), "   <- Python rounds exact halves to the EVEN neighbour")
max(0, 73) = 73    max(0, -4) = 0round(2.5) = 2    round(3.5) = 4    <- Python rounds exact halves to the EVEN neighbour

(The half-to-even rule has probability zero of mattering for a continuous draw, but you may be surprised if you test round(2.5) yourself.)

Reading nested Python: the compact version¶

The provided model does all four steps in one line:

demand = max(0, int(round(rng.normal(demand_mean, demand_sd))))

Read nested function calls from the inside out:

  1. rng.normal(demand_mean, demand_sd) → raw draw, e.g. 73.02
  2. round( ... ) → 73
  3. int( ... ) → 73 as an integer
  4. max(0, ... ) → 73 (or 0 if it were negative)

Check that it gives exactly the same demand when we restart the same stream:

In [59]:
check_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)demand_compact = max(    0,    int(        round(            check_rng.normal(demand_mean, demand_sd)        )    ))print("step-by-step demand:", demand, "   compact demand:", demand_compact)
step-by-step demand: 73    compact demand: 73

Spending: one random value per customer¶

Each of the $D$ customers spends a random amount. We draw all $D$ spends at once with size=demand.

In [60]:
spend_mean = regular["spend_mean"]spend_sd = regular["spend_sd"]raw_spending = manual_rng.normal(spend_mean, spend_sd, size=demand)raw_spending[:10]
Out[60]:
array([6.26626079, 5.28946598, 4.89863337, 6.33206265, 6.03677006,       5.08024045, 4.87098365, 6.24591668, 6.33920122, 5.65742515])
In [61]:

number of spending values: 73    demand: 73smallest spend: 4.307243029316745    largest spend: 7.803174890836568

len(raw_spending) equals demand: one spend per customer. This is why the model uses size=demand, and why demand must be a non-negative integer.

Clipping spending at zero: np.maximum¶

With this seed no spend is negative, so to see what clipping does we use a tiny made-up array.

In [62]:
example = np.array([5.2, -0.4, 6.1])np.maximum(0, example)
Out[62]:
array([5.2, 0. , 6.1])
  • max(0, x) (built-in) is for one number.
  • np.maximum(0, array) is the elementwise version for arrays.

Apply it to the real spends:

In [63]:
spending = np.maximum(0, raw_spending)print("any values changed by clipping?", (spending != raw_spending).any())
any values changed by clipping? False

Clipping is not truncation¶

  • Clipping at 0: draw from the Normal, and if the value is negative, replace it by 0. The result has a point mass at exactly 0.
  • Truncation at 0: draw from the Normal conditioned on being positive (throw negatives away and redraw). The result is never exactly 0 and has a different, larger mean.

A small illustration with a distribution where negatives are common, $N(0.5,1)$:

In [64]:
illus_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED + 6)x_illus = illus_rng.normal(0.5, 1.0, size=100_000)clipped = np.maximum(0, x_illus)truncated = x_illus[x_illus > 0]pd.Series({    "fraction of draws that were negative": np.mean(x_illus < 0),    "mean after CLIPPING (negatives -> 0)": clipped.mean(),    "mean after TRUNCATION (negatives discarded)": truncated.mean(),})
Out[64]:
fraction of draws that were negative           0.308610mean after CLIPPING (negatives -> 0)           0.697279mean after TRUNCATION (negatives discarded)    1.008517dtype: float64

The two means differ, so the two models are different. In our kiosk it does not matter numerically, because negative values are astronomically unlikely:

In [65]:
def normal_below(x, mean, sd):    """P(N(mean, sd^2) < x), computed accurately in the far tail."""    return 0.5 * math.erfc((mean - x) / (sd * np.sqrt(2)))pd.Series({    "P(regular demand rounds below 0)": normal_below(-0.5, 70, 10),    "P(coupon demand rounds below 0)": normal_below(-0.5, 86, 16),    "P(regular spend < 0)": normal_below(0, 6.0, 0.8),    "P(coupon spend < 0)": normal_below(0, 5.7, 0.9),})
Out[65]:
P(regular demand rounds below 0)    8.945890e-13P(coupon demand rounds below 0)     3.217898e-08P(regular spend < 0)                3.190892e-14P(coupon spend < 0)                 1.199602e-10dtype: float64

The largest of these probabilities is about $3\times10^{-8}$ (coupon demand, whose mean is $86.5/16\approx5.4$ SDs above $-0.5$). In this model the clipping is a safety guard, not a feature that changes the results — but it is still clipping, not truncation.

Revenue: a sum of a random number of random terms¶

$$R=\sum_{j=1}^{D}S_j .$$

Both the number of terms $D$ and each term $S_j$ are random. This is the one structural feature not present in the integration example.

In [66]:
revenue = spending.sum()revenue
Out[66]:
np.float64(434.5969464099002)

Only now: package the calculation into a function¶

All this function does is package the calculation we have just performed by hand.

In [72]:
def simulate_kiosk_day(assumptions, rng, return_details=False):    """Simulate ONE day at the kiosk and return its profit (or a dictionary of details)."""    demand = max(0, int(round(rng.normal(assumptions["demand_mean"], assumptions["demand_sd"]))))    spending = np.maximum(0, rng.normal(assumptions["spend_mean"], assumptions["spend_sd"], demand))    revenue = spending.sum()    variable_cost = assumptions["variable_cost"] * demand    total_cost = variable_cost + assumptions["fixed_cost"] + assumptions["campaign_cost"]    profit = revenue - total_cost    if return_details:        return {            "demand": demand,            "revenue": revenue,            "total_cost": total_cost,            "profit": profit,        }    return profit

Map each line of the function back to the manual cells¶

Function lineManual cells above
demand = max(0, int(round(rng.normal(...))))raw_demand → rounded_demand → integer_demand → demand
spending = np.maximum(0, rng.normal(..., demand))raw_spending (with size=demand) → spending
revenue = spending.sum()revenue
variable_cost = assumptions["variable_cost"] * demandvariable_cost_per_customer * demand
total_cost = ... + assumptions["fixed_cost"] + assumptions["campaign_cost"]total_cost
profit = revenue - total_costprofit

The only differences: the function looks values up in assumptions directly instead of copying them into separate variables first, and the third argument of rng.normal is demand written positionally instead of size=demand (same meaning).

Test: with the same seed, the function must reproduce the hand calculation exactly, because it draws the same random numbers in the same order.

In [73]:
test_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)print("profit from the function :", simulate_kiosk_day(regular, test_rng))print("profit by hand           :", profit)
profit from the function : 72.09694640990023profit by hand           : 72.09694640990023

What does return_details=False do?¶

return_details is a Boolean (True/False) parameter with default False.

  • Default call → the function returns just the profit, one number. This is what a Monte Carlo run needs thousands of times.
  • return_details=True → the if block runs and the function returns a dictionary with demand, revenue, cost and profit. This is what we want when checking or debugging, to see that the pieces make sense.

(When return runs inside the if block, the function ends there; the final return profit is not reached.)

In [74]:
simulate_kiosk_day(regular, np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED))
Out[74]:
np.float64(72.09694640990023)
In [75]:
simulate_kiosk_day(regular, np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED), return_details=True)
Out[75]:
{'demand': 73, 'revenue': np.float64(434.5969464099002), 'total_cost': 362.5, 'profit': np.float64(72.09694640990023)}

Demo 6: Several kiosk days, then many¶

Three days by hand¶

In [77]:

Same model, same parameters, same generator — different profits, because the generator moves forward along its stream on each call. That is what we want: three independent days.

Five days with a loop, collecting the results¶

In [78]:
day_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)profits = []for replication in range(1, 6):    profit = simulate_kiosk_day(regular, day_rng)    profits.append(profit)    print(f"after replication {replication}: the list has {len(profits)} profit(s)")profits
after replication 1: the list has 1 profit(s)after replication 2: the list has 2 profit(s)after replication 3: the list has 3 profit(s)after replication 4: the list has 4 profit(s)after replication 5: the list has 5 profit(s)

[np.float64(72.09694640990023), np.float64(99.20796736883034), np.float64(39.74601254294345), np.float64(72.30383382580192), np.float64(52.6956639808638)]
  • range(1, 6) gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — five iterations. The upper endpoint 6 is excluded, so that range(1, n + 1) gives exactly $n$ values numbered $1,\dots,n$.
  • The first three entries equal profit_1, profit_2, profit_3: the loop does what we did by hand.

Now the average:

In [79]:
np.mean(profits)
Out[79]:
np.float64(67.21008482566795)

This is

$$\bar H_5=\frac15\sum_{i=1}^5 H_i ,$$

a (very imprecise) Monte Carlo estimate of $\mathbb E[H]$ — the exact same structure as $\hat I_n$ in Demo 1.

Python lesson: looping over pairs, and tuple unpacking¶

We want to repeat the whole experiment for two scenarios. Each scenario has a name and a dictionary of assumptions. We pair them in a tuple ("Regular", regular).

In [80]:
pair = ("Regular", regular)case, assumptions = pairprint("case =", case)print("assumptions['campaign_cost'] =", assumptions["campaign_cost"])
case = Regularassumptions['campaign_cost'] = 0
In [81]:
for case, assumptions in [("Regular", regular), ("Coupon", coupon)]:    print(f"case = {case:8s}   campaign cost = {assumptions['campaign_cost']}")
case = Regular    campaign cost = 0case = Coupon     campaign cost = 30
  • Iteration 1: case = "Regular", assumptions = regular.
  • Iteration 2: case = "Coupon", assumptions = coupon.

Python lesson: nested loops¶

Inside each scenario we repeat the day many times. A loop inside another loop is a nested loop:

Regular                  <- outer loop, iteration 1    replication 1        <- inner loop runs completely    replication 2    ...    replication nCoupon                   <- outer loop, iteration 2    replication 1        <- inner loop runs completely again    replication 2    ...    replication n

The inner loop runs completely for each single iteration of the outer loop. A tiny version that only prints:

In [82]:
for case, assumptions in [("Regular", regular), ("Coupon", coupon)]:    print(case)    for replication in range(1, 4):        print("    replication", replication)
Regular    replication 1    replication 2    replication 3Coupon    replication 1    replication 2    replication 3

Total number of inner iterations = $2\times3=6$. With 1,000 replications per case it is 2,000.

Only now: the experiment function¶

It is the nested loop above, with print replaced by "simulate a day and store a row".

In [83]:
def run_kiosk_experiment(n_replications, seed):    """Simulate n_replications days for each case. One row per simulated day."""    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)    rows = []    for case, assumptions in [("Regular", regular), ("Coupon", coupon)]:        for replication in range(1, n_replications + 1):            rows.append({                "replication": replication,                "case": case,                "profit": simulate_kiosk_day(assumptions, rng),            })    return pd.DataFrame(rows)
In [84]:

Demo 7: Estimating a probability with indicator variables¶

A tiny example first¶

Five made-up daily profits:

In [92]:
example_profits = np.array([50, -20, 10, -5, 30])example_profits < 0
Out[92]:
array([False,  True, False,  True, False])

Each entry answers the question "was this a loss-making day?". Convert True/False into 1/0:

In [93]:
(example_profits < 0).astype(int)
Out[93]:
array([0, 1, 0, 1, 0])
In [94]:
(example_profits < 0).mean()
Out[94]:
np.float64(0.4)

Check by hand: two of the five days are losses, so the proportion is $\frac{0+1+0+1+0}{5}=\frac25=0.4$. The mean of an indicator is a proportion.

The theory: every probability is an expectation¶

For an event $A$, the indicator is

$$\mathbf 1_A=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }A\text{ happens},\\0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

It is a random variable taking only the values 0 and 1, so

$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=1\cdot\mathbb P(A)+0\cdot\mathbb P(A^c)=\mathbb P(A).$$

With $A=\{H<0\}$ and $Y_i=\mathbf 1\{H_i<0\}$:

$$\hat p=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1\{H_i<0\}=\text{fraction of simulated days that lose money}.$$

This is the same Monte Carlo estimator $\bar Y_n$ as before, with $h(X)=\mathbf 1\{\text{profit}(X)<0\}$. So the LLN, CLT, SE and CI all apply unchanged. For a 0/1 variable $\mathrm{Var}(Y)=p(1-p)$, so $\mathrm{SE}(\hat p)\approx\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)/n}$.

Demo 8: Confidence interval for mean profit — by hand first¶

We compute the 95% CI for $\mathbb E[H]$ under the Regular policy, one line at a time, exactly as in Demo 2.

$$\bar H_n\pm1.96\,\frac{s_H}{\sqrt n}.$$

In [100]:

1000
In [101]:

Out[101]:

Out[103]:

z = 1.96margin = z * standard_errorlower = mean - marginupper = mean + marginprint(f"estimate = {mean:.2f},  SE = {standard_error:.3f},  margin = {margin:.3f}")print(f"95% CI for expected Regular profit: [{lower:.2f}, {upper:.2f}],  width = {upper - lower:.3f}")
estimate = 64.17,  SE = 1.152,  margin = 2.25995% CI for expected Regular profit: [61.91, 66.43],  width = 4.518

Interpretation (word it carefully).

"Under this model, the expected daily profit of the Regular policy is estimated at about [estimate]. An approximate 95% confidence interval is [lower, upper]. If we repeated this whole 1,000-day simulation many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the model's true expected profit."

Notice how the numbers compare (DEMO_SEED = 6901): the sample SD of daily profits is about 36, but the standard error is only about 1.15 — smaller by the factor $\sqrt{1000}\approx31.6$. Daily profits vary a lot; our estimate of their average is precise.

We need exactly the same calculation for Coupon, and later for many other experiments. So now a function becomes useful.

In [105]:
def mean_confidence_interval(values, z=1.96):    """Approximate CI for the mean: mean +/- z * s / sqrt(n)."""    values = np.asarray(values)    mean = values.mean()    sample_sd = values.std(ddof=1)    standard_error = sample_sd / np.sqrt(len(values))    lower = mean - z * standard_error    upper = mean + z * standard_error    return mean, sample_sd, standard_error, lower, upper, upper - lower
  • return a, b, c, ... returns several values packed into one tuple.
  • The caller unpacks them into separate names, in the same order — exactly like case, assumptions = pair in Demo 6.

Check against the manual calculation:

In [106]:
mean_r, sd_r, se_r, lower_r, upper_r, width_r = mean_confidence_interval(regular_profits)print("function:", round(lower_r, 4), round(upper_r, 4))print("by hand :", round(lower, 4), round(upper, 4))
function: 61.9135 66.431by hand : 61.9135 66.431

Now both cases, with a loop over the groups:

A CI for the mean is NOT a range for individual days¶

Question: "The Coupon CI is only a few units wide. Does that mean 95% of Coupon days have profit inside it?"

Test it directly: what fraction of the 1,000 simulated Coupon days fall inside the Coupon CI? And what range does contain the middle 95% of days?

Demo 9: How many replications? The $O(n^{-1/2})$ rate for the kiosk¶

We repeat the complete experiment with 100, 1,000 and 10,000 replications, re-creating the generator from DEMO_SEED at the start of each full experiment so the comparison is reproducible. (Because every experiment starts from the same seed, the 100-day run is the start of the 1,000-day run, and so on: these are nested views of one stream, not independent checks.)

Predict first. Suppose the SE for mean profit at $n=100$ is $a$. Using $\mathrm{SE}\propto1/\sqrt n$:

  • at $n=1000$: SE $\approx$ ?
  • at $n=10000$: SE $\approx$ ?
In [110]:
stability_rows = []for n_replications in [100, 1000, 10000]:    experiment = run_kiosk_experiment(n_replications=n_replications, seed=DEMO_SEED)    for case, group in experiment.groupby("case"):        mean, sample_sd, standard_error, lower, upper, width = mean_confidence_interval(group["profit"])        stability_rows.append({            "replications": n_replications,            "case": case,            "mean": mean,            "sample_sd": sample_sd,            "standard_error": standard_error,            "ci_width": width,        })stability_demo = pd.DataFrame(stability_rows)stability_demo

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))for case, group in stability_demo.groupby("case"):    ax.plot(group["replications"], group["ci_width"], marker="o", label=case)ax.set_xscale("log")ax.set_yscale("log")ax.set_xlabel("Replications n")ax.set_ylabel("95% CI width")ax.set_title("More replications reduce Monte Carlo uncertainty (slope -1/2)")ax.legend()plt.show()

The widths shrink roughly as $1/\sqrt n$ (a straight line of slope $-1/2$ on log–log axes). More replications reduce simulation noise; they cannot repair unrealistic demand, spending, cost or capacity assumptions.

Demo 9b: Does the CLT apply to the kiosk?¶

Demo 3 showed the bell shape for an integral, which invites a fair objection: "that says nothing about the business". So we rerun the whole 1,000-replication Coupon experiment 200 times and look at the 200 answers we could have reported.

Two levels of repetition:

experiment 1:   day 1, day 2, ..., day 1000   ->  mean of 1000 profits  ->  one estimate  H-bar^(1)experiment 2:   day 1, day 2, ..., day 1000   ->  one estimate  H-bar^(2)...experiment 200: day 1, day 2, ..., day 1000   ->  one estimate  H-bar^(200)

The explicit nested loop (read this version first)¶

In [114]:
kiosk_repeat_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)coupon_means = []coupon_bad_fractions = []for experiment in range(200):    daily_profits = []    for day in range(1000):        profit = simulate_kiosk_day(coupon, kiosk_repeat_rng)        daily_profits.append(profit)    experiment_mean = np.mean(daily_profits)    coupon_means.append(experiment_mean)    coupon_bad_fractions.append(np.mean(np.array(daily_profits) < 0))coupon_means = np.array(coupon_means)coupon_bad_fractions = np.array(coupon_bad_fractions)print("number of estimates:", len(coupon_means))print("first five estimates:", coupon_means[:5].round(2))
number of estimates: 200first five estimates: [68.16 66.52 63.54 66.75 65.09]

Every level has a meaning:

CodeMeaning
inner loop over daythe individual simulated days $H_1,\dots,H_{1000}$
experiment_meanone Monte Carlo estimate $\bar H_{1000}$
outer loop over experimentrepeating the entire experiment
coupon_means200 draws from the sampling distribution of the estimator $\bar H_{1000}$

daily_profits = [] is inside the outer loop on purpose: each experiment must start with an empty list.

Question: What would go wrong if daily_profits = [] were written once, before the outer loop?

Does the spread of the 200 estimates match the CLT prediction?¶

In [115]:
coupon_sd = coupon_profits.std()pd.Series({    "mean of the 200 reported means": coupon_means.mean(),    "SD of the 200 reported means (observed)": coupon_means.std(ddof=1),    "CLT prediction  s_H / sqrt(1000)": coupon_sd / np.sqrt(1000),    "SD of individual Coupon days  s_H": coupon_sd,}).round(4)
Out[115]:
mean of the 200 reported means             65.0235SD of the 200 reported means (observed)     1.5285CLT prediction  s_H / sqrt(1000)            1.5708SD of individual Coupon days  s_H          49.6746dtype: float64

Question: How close is the observed SD of the 200 means to the CLT prediction $s_H/\sqrt{1000}$? How does it compare with the SD of individual days?

The side-by-side picture — one of the most important in the course¶

Question (think before running the next cells): "What exactly is one observation in the left histogram? In the right histogram?"

In [116]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))axes[0].hist(coupon_profits, bins=25, alpha=0.7, color="tab:blue", edgecolor="white")axes[0].set_title(r"Individual daily profits $H$  (1,000 simulated days)")axes[0].set_xlabel("Profit on one day")axes[1].hist(coupon_means, bins=20, alpha=0.7, color="tab:orange", edgecolor="white")axes[1].set_title(r"Estimated mean $\bar H_{1000}$  (200 whole experiments)")axes[1].set_xlabel("Mean daily profit over 1,000 days")for ax in axes:    ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")plt.tight_layout()plt.show()
In [117]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))ax.hist(coupon_profits, bins=25, density=True, alpha=0.6, color="tab:blue", label=r"daily profits $H$")ax.hist(coupon_means, bins=20, density=True, alpha=0.8, color="tab:orange", label=r"estimates $\bar H_{1000}$")ax.set_xlabel("profit")ax.set_ylabel("density")ax.set_title("The same two distributions on a COMMON axis")ax.legend()plt.show()

On a common axis the sampling distribution is a thin spike inside the wide distribution of daily profits: its SD is $\sqrt{1000}\approx32$ times smaller.

An honest caveat about shape. In this particular model the daily profit $H$ is itself close to Normal (its sample skewness is essentially 0), because profit is dominated by the Normal demand draw. So the kiosk picture above demonstrates the width part of the CLT ($\sigma/\sqrt n$) convincingly, but not the shape part — both histograms are bell-shaped for different reasons. The shape part was shown in Demo 3 with the skewed $e^U$. To see it for the kiosk, use an output that is obviously non-Normal: the bad-day indicator $\mathbf 1\{H<0\}$, which takes only the values 0 and 1.

FeatureIndividual profit $H$Estimated mean $\bar H_n$
What is one observation?one simulated dayone whole Monte Carlo experiment ($n$ days)
Centre$\mathbb E[H]$$\mathbb E[H]$
SD$\sigma_H$$\sigma_H/\sqrt n$
Shapewhatever the model produces (here close to Normal; for the indicator below, two spikes at 0 and 1)approximately Normal, by the CLT
Meaningbusiness variability: how different one day is from anotherMonte Carlo estimation uncertainty: how much our reported answer would move if we reran the study
Described bySD of daily profit, $\mathbb P(H<0)$SE, confidence interval

Questions:

  1. "The coupon CI for the mean is a few units wide. Does that mean 95% of days fall in a few-unit range?"
  2. "Why can daily profits be non-Normal while the sample means look Normal?"
In [118]:
coupon_indicator = (coupon_profits < 0).astype(int)fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))axes[0].bar([0, 1], [np.mean(coupon_indicator == 0), np.mean(coupon_indicator == 1)],            width=0.4, color="grey")axes[0].set_xticks([0, 1])axes[0].set_title(r"Individual indicator $\mathbf{1}\{H<0\}$: only 0 or 1")axes[0].set_xlabel("value on one day")axes[0].set_ylabel("proportion of days")axes[1].hist(coupon_bad_fractions, bins=15, color="tab:orange", edgecolor="white")axes[1].set_title(r"200 estimates $\hat p$ of $P(H<0)$, each from 1,000 days")axes[1].set_xlabel("estimated bad-day probability")axes[1].set_ylabel("Frequency")plt.tight_layout()plt.show()p_bar = coupon_bad_fractions.mean()print(f"SD of the 200 estimates p-hat: {coupon_bad_fractions.std(ddof=1):.4f}")print(f"CLT prediction sqrt(p(1-p)/1000) with p = {p_bar:.3f}: {np.sqrt(p_bar * (1 - p_bar) / 1000):.4f}")
SD of the 200 estimates p-hat: 0.0093CLT prediction sqrt(p(1-p)/1000) with p = 0.104: 0.0097

Here the contrast is unmistakable: one observation of the indicator is 0 or 1 — as far from Normal as a distribution can be — yet the average of 1,000 of them is bell-shaped around $\mathbb P(H<0)\approx0.1$, with SD close to $\sqrt{p(1-p)/1000}$. This is the shape part of the CLT, for the kiosk.

Optional: the compact version with list comprehensions¶

The same nested loop can be written in one expression using list comprehensions. It is equivalent, but harder for beginners to read, so the explicit loop above is the version to learn from.

coupon_means = np.array([    np.mean([simulate_kiosk_day(coupon, kiosk_repeat_rng) for _ in range(1000)])    for _ in range(200)])

[expression for _ in range(k)] means "evaluate expression $k$ times and collect the results in a list". Check equivalence on the first five experiments (restarting the same stream):

In [119]:
check_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)compact_first_five = np.array([    np.mean([simulate_kiosk_day(coupon, check_rng) for _ in range(1000)])    for _ in range(5)])print(compact_first_five.round(4))print(coupon_means[:5].round(4))print("identical?", np.allclose(compact_first_five, coupon_means[:5]))
[68.1637 66.5224 63.5364 66.7524 65.0947][68.1637 66.5224 63.5364 66.7524 65.0947]identical? True

Demo 10: Controlled sensitivity to the campaign cost¶

Question: how do mean profit and loss probability change if the coupon campaign costs 0, 15, 30, 45 or 60?

We do one comparison (cost 0 versus cost 15) by hand before writing a loop. Along the way we need two Python ideas: copying a dictionary, and resetting a seed on purpose.

Python lesson: why .copy()?¶

We want a modified coupon scenario without damaging the original coupon. A toy example shows the danger.

In [120]:
toy = {"campaign_cost": 30}alias = toyalias["campaign_cost"] = 15print("toy after changing alias:", toy)
toy after changing alias: {'campaign_cost': 15}
In [121]:
toy = {"campaign_cost": 30}safe_copy = toy.copy()safe_copy["campaign_cost"] = 15print("toy after changing safe_copy:", toy)print("safe_copy:", safe_copy)
toy after changing safe_copy: {'campaign_cost': 30}safe_copy: {'campaign_cost': 15}

If we wrote changed_coupon = coupon and then changed changed_coupon["campaign_cost"], we would silently change coupon itself, and every later cell that uses coupon would use the wrong campaign cost.

Cost 0 versus cost 15, by hand¶

We will need "simulate many days and collect the profits" several times, so we first write that loop once more — explicitly.

In [122]:
coupon_cost_0 = coupon.copy()coupon_cost_0["campaign_cost"] = 0rng_cost_0 = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)profits_cost_0 = []for day in range(2000):    profits_cost_0.append(simulate_kiosk_day(coupon_cost_0, rng_cost_0))profits_cost_0 = np.array(profits_cost_0)print(f"campaign cost  0: mean profit = {profits_cost_0.mean():.3f},  P(loss) = {np.mean(profits_cost_0 < 0):.4f}")
campaign cost  0: mean profit = 97.343,  P(loss) = 0.0285
In [123]:
coupon_cost_15 = coupon.copy()coupon_cost_15["campaign_cost"] = 15rng_cost_15 = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)profits_cost_15 = []for day in range(2000):    profits_cost_15.append(simulate_kiosk_day(coupon_cost_15, rng_cost_15))profits_cost_15 = np.array(profits_cost_15)print(f"campaign cost 15: mean profit = {profits_cost_15.mean():.3f},  P(loss) = {np.mean(profits_cost_15 < 0):.4f}")
campaign cost 15: mean profit = 82.343,  P(loss) = 0.0575
In [124]:
day_by_day_difference = profits_cost_15 - profits_cost_0print("first five day-by-day differences:", day_by_day_difference[:5])print("difference in mean profit        :", profits_cost_15.mean() - profits_cost_0.mean())print("every day exactly 15 lower?      :", np.allclose(day_by_day_difference, -15))
first five day-by-day differences: [-15. -15. -15. -15. -15.]difference in mean profit        : -15.0every day exactly 15 lower?      : True

What happened? Because both runs started from the same seed, and campaign cost does not affect any random draw, the two runs simulated the same 2,000 days — same demand, same spending — and the only difference is the campaign cost. Every day is exactly 15 lower, so the difference in means is exactly 15, with no Monte Carlo noise at all in the comparison.

Compare: the same comparison with independent streams¶

In [125]:
rng_a = np.random.default_rng(1001)rng_b = np.random.default_rng(2002)indep_0 = []indep_15 = []for day in range(2000):    indep_0.append(simulate_kiosk_day(coupon_cost_0, rng_a))    indep_15.append(simulate_kiosk_day(coupon_cost_15, rng_b))indep_0 = np.array(indep_0)indep_15 = np.array(indep_15)se_difference = np.sqrt(indep_0.var(ddof=1) / 2000 + indep_15.var(ddof=1) / 2000)print(f"independent streams: difference in mean profit = {indep_15.mean() - indep_0.mean():.3f}   (true effect: -15)")print(f"SE of that difference is about {se_difference:.2f}")
independent streams: difference in mean profit = -14.130   (true effect: -15)SE of that difference is about 1.67

With independent streams the estimated effect is $-15$ plus noise of a couple of units, because the two runs saw different random days. With the same seed, the comparison isolates the effect of the one parameter we changed.

Good seed resetting versus bad seed resetting¶

Bad: resetting inside every simulated dayDeliberate: same seed for each scenario being compared
What is resetthe generator, at the start of every replicationthe generator, at the start of each whole scenario run
Effectevery "replication" is the same day; $s=0$, CI width 0 — fake certaintyeach scenario sees the same sequence of random days
Purposenone — it is a buga controlled comparison (also called common random numbers): differences are attributable to the changed parameter

Here is the bug, so that you can recognise it:

In [126]:
def buggy_simulate_kiosk_day(assumptions):    rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)    return simulate_kiosk_day(assumptions, rng)buggy_profits = []for day in range(5):    buggy_profits.append(buggy_simulate_kiosk_day(coupon))print("five 'different' days:", np.round(buggy_profits, 3))print("sample SD of these days:", np.std(buggy_profits, ddof=1))
five 'different' days: [75.061 75.061 75.061 75.061 75.061]sample SD of these days: 0.0

Five identical days, SD 0, so the "confidence interval" would have width 0 — a precise answer to the wrong question.

Only now: the loop over campaign costs¶

In [127]:
sensitivity_rows = []for campaign_cost in [0, 15, 30, 45, 60]:    changed_coupon = coupon.copy()    changed_coupon["campaign_cost"] = campaign_cost    sensitivity_rng = np.random.default_rng(DEMO_SEED)    profits = []    for day in range(2000):        profits.append(simulate_kiosk_day(changed_coupon, sensitivity_rng))    profits = np.array(profits)    sensitivity_rows.append({        "campaign_cost": campaign_cost,        "mean_profit": profits.mean(),        "bad_day_probability": np.mean(profits < 0),    })sensitivity_demo = pd.DataFrame(sensitivity_rows)sensitivity_demo

Questions:

  1. Check that the first two rows match the by-hand cost-0 and cost-15 runs above.
  2. By how much does mean profit fall for each extra 15 of campaign cost? Why is the fall exactly the same at every step?
  3. Does the loss probability rise linearly with the campaign cost? Why or why not?
  4. Earlier we said that resetting the seed is a bug. Why is it legitimate to reset it here?

Demo 11: A strong interpretation¶

The evidence from Demos 6–8 (DEMO_SEED = 6901, 1,000 days per case):

RegularCoupon
estimated mean profit64.265.4
95% CI for mean profit[61.9, 66.4][62.3, 68.4]
SD of daily profit3650
estimated $\mathbb P(\text{loss})$0.042 [0.030, 0.054]0.095 [0.077, 0.113]

The two CIs for mean profit overlap heavily: at this $n$ the simulation cannot tell the two expected profits apart. The loss probabilities, by contrast, are clearly different — their CIs do not overlap.

Under this model, the coupon and regular cases have similar estimated mean profit, but the coupon has a much wider daily-profit distribution and a higher probability of loss. I would not adopt the coupon unchanged. I would test a lower campaign cost or run a short pilot, then replace the assumed demand response with observed transaction data. This conclusion is conditional on the Normal demand and spending assumptions and ignores queue capacity and customers who leave.

A strong recommendation connects five things:

  1. expected return — the estimated $\mathbb E[H]$ for each option;
  2. downside risk — the estimated $\mathbb P(H<0)$ (and the spread of daily profit);
  3. Monte Carlo uncertainty — the confidence intervals: are the two means distinguishable given the SEs?
  4. model limitations — which assumptions could be wrong, and which direction that would push the answer;
  5. a practical next action — pilot, collect data, test a cheaper campaign.

Points 3 and 4 are different kinds of uncertainty. Point 3 shrinks with more replications; point 4 does not.

Final theory map¶

$$X_i\;\longrightarrow\;Y_i=h(X_i)\qquad\qquadY_1,\dots,Y_n\;\longrightarrow\;\bar Y_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i$$

LLN (where the estimate goes):$$\bar Y_n\to\mathbb E[Y].$$

Variance of the mean (from independence):$$\mathrm{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\frac{\mathrm{Var}(Y)}{n}.$$

CLT (how the estimate is spread):$$\bar Y_n\approx N\!\left(\mathbb E[Y],\ \frac{\mathrm{Var}(Y)}{n}\right).$$

Estimated standard error:$$\mathrm{SE}=\frac{s}{\sqrt n},\qquad s^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum(Y_i-\bar Y)^2 \quad(\texttt{ddof=1}).$$

Approximate 95% CI:$$\bar Y_n\pm1.96\,\mathrm{SE},\qquad \mathbb P(-1.96<Z<1.96)\approx0.95.$$

Rate: $\mathrm{SE}=O(n^{-1/2})$ — 4× replications halves the SE, 100× gives one more decimal place.

Probability as an expectation: for an event $A$,$$\mathbb P(A)=\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A],\qquad \hat p=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1_{A,i}.$$

The same formulas in the three problems of this demo¶

$X$$Y=h(X)$targetestimator
Monte Carlo integration$U\sim\mathrm{U}(0,1)$$e^U$$\int_0^1e^u\,du=e-1$$\frac1n\sum e^{U_i}$
Mean kiosk profitdemand and spends for one dayprofit $H$$\mathbb E[H]$$\bar H_n$
Probability of a loss-making daydemand and spends for one day$\mathbf 1\{H<0\}$$\mathbb P(H<0)$fraction of simulated days with $H<0$

In all three rows: the LLN justifies the estimator, the CLT justifies the error bar $\pm1.96\,s/\sqrt n$, and the error shrinks like $n^{-1/2}$.

Distinctions to leave with¶

This …… is not this
one output $H_i$the expected output $\mathbb E[H]$
sample SD $s_H$ (variation of days)standard error $s_H/\sqrt n$ (uncertainty of the mean)
distribution of $H$sampling distribution of $\bar H_n$
LLN: $\bar H_n\to\mathbb E[H]$CLT: $\frac{\bar H_n-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\approx N(0,1)$
CI for $\mathbb E[H]$a range containing 95% of daily profits
Monte Carlo error (shrinks with $n$)model error (does not)
clipping max(0, x)sampling from a truncated Normal

Final coding map¶

One random draw    ↓One model output                         u_small, h_small            (Demo 1)    ↓                                     raw_demand → demand → profit (Demo 5)Repeat manually a few times              n = 10 block, n = 100 block (Demo 2)    ↓                                     profit_1, profit_2, profit_3 (Demo 6)Loop                                     for n in [...]:  /  for replication in range(1, 6):    ↓Same calculation needed repeatedly    ↓Function                                 repeated_estimates, simulate_kiosk_day,    ↓                                     run_kiosk_experiment, mean_confidence_intervalMany outputs    ↓Mean / SD / probability                  .mean(), .std(ddof=1), (profit < 0).mean(), groupby    ↓Repeat the entire experiment             outer loop in Demo 3 and Demo 9b    ↓Sampling distribution    ↓CLT / SE / confidence interval           s / sqrt(n),  estimate ± 1.96 SE,  coverage

Rule of thumb for your own code: write the long, readable version first; print the intermediate values; check them against the mathematics; only then wrap the calculation in a loop or function — and test the function on a tiny case before using it at scale.

Before you start Lab 4¶

You should now be able to explain:

  1. what $X$, $h(X)$ and $\mathbb E[h(X)]$ mean in an integration or profit problem;
  2. why one simulated day is not a decision;
  3. why the LLN makes the average converge, and why the error need not fall at every step;
  4. the difference between the sample SD and the standard error, and why we use ddof=1;
  5. that a Monte Carlo estimate is itself random, approximately Normal about the true value with SD $\sigma_h/\sqrt n$ (CLT);
  6. what "95% confident" claims — the interval is random and captures the fixed target about 95% of the time;
  7. why a confidence interval for the mean is not a range for individual days;
  8. how an indicator average estimates a probability;
  9. why interval width shrinks approximately as $1/\sqrt n$, so 100 times the replications buys 10 times the precision;
  10. why more replications cannot validate unrealistic assumptions.

Items 5, 6 and 9 are assessed in Lab 4 parts A2, A3 and F. Do not skip Demos 3 and 9b.

The daily-profit model in the lab is provided already written. You read, run and explain it rather than building it — Demo 5 is your preparation for that.

Common errors¶

  • Resetting the generator inside the daily simulation function, which repeats the same day (Demo 10).
  • Treating one simulated output as an expected value.
  • Reading the spread of individual daily profits off the confidence interval for the mean, or the reverse — the two histograms in Demo 9b are the cure.
  • Expecting the sampling distribution of the estimate to look like the distribution of the underlying outputs.
  • Allowing negative demand or spending without explanation, or calling the clipping "truncation".
  • Comparing only mean profit and ignoring downside risk.
  • Using NumPy's default std() (ddof = 0) instead of the sample SD (ddof=1) in the confidence interval.
  • Confusing sample SD with the standard error of the mean.
  • Saying "there is a 95% chance the true value lies in this interval" instead of describing the procedure's long-run coverage.
  • Assuming absolute integration error must fall monotonically as $n$ grows.
  • Claiming that more replications validate the model assumptions.
  • Changing a scenario dictionary without .copy(), which silently changes the original.
  • Changing several assumptions at once and attributing the result to one input.
